title.title: Matrix multiplication with exponent at most $9/4$
title.subtitle: Claim: two $n \times n$ complex matrices multiply in $O(n^{9/4+\varepsilon})$ operations

beats.text: Schoolbook: each entry of $C$ costs $n$ products, $n^3$ in all
Since 1990 the best exponent $\omega$ crept from 2.3755 to 2.3712
The claim, $\omega \le 2.25$, is a bigger drop than the previous thirty-six years combined

plain: Multiplying two big tables of numbers takes about $n^3$ steps; the question is how far below that you can go

steps: Give every way of multiplying a single score
One rule pushes the score up from below
Squeezed between them, the exponent can be at most 9/4

voice.text: The schoolbook way takes n cubed steps. Since nineteen ninety, the record barely moved.
The proof scores every method, then squeezes that score from both sides.
Claimed: omega at most nine over four.
